description: Card Description (Short) A feature-packed 65% budget mechanical keyboard boasting a gasket mount, tri-mode wireless, a unique LCD display, and an ergonomic volume slider for just $50.
metaDescription: The AJAZZ AK650 punches way above its weight class, offering premium features like a flex-cut polycarbonate plate, 5-pin hot-swappable PCB, and a rare display and slider combo in a tight 65% form factor. An absolute dream for Windows users on a budget.
detailedDescription:
AJAZZ AK650 Detailed Review

If there is a Swiss Army Knife of mechanical keyboards, the AJAZZ AK650 might just be it. We are talking about a keyboard that features a gasket mount, tri-mode wireless connectivity, a hot-swap PCB, double-shot PBT keycaps, great switches, and—best of all—a built-in display and volume slider. All of this comes in at just 50 bucks (approx. 6,500 BDT). Positioned as AJAZZ's brand new 65% keyboard, it brings tier-one specifications across all fronts into a budget-friendly package.

Design & Build Quality

The case is constructed from durable ABS plastic with smooth rounded corners and a subtle gradient back. Up at the top right, we get a unique display and knob combo that you rarely see on tight form-factor boards. It comes in two colorways and keycap options: side-printed shine-through or non-shine-through cherry-profile PBT keycaps. Both are double-shot with decent thickness, making them feel great to type on while looking sharp. Normally, fitting a display and a knob onto a cramped 65% keyboard forces you to lose at least two keys. To solve this, AJAZZ integrated an 0.85-inch LCD display at the top right corner right next to a slim, ergonomic volume slider. The volume slider feels satisfying with clear tactile feedback when adjusted.

Display & Customization

The built-in display shows the time, date, battery life, and connection mode, while also letting you navigate settings like pairing or RGB adjustments. For an extra bit of flair, you can upload your own custom GIFs using the proprietary Windows software. While the software lets you remap secondary layers, set macros, and control the vibrant RGB lighting, it is strictly Windows-only. There is a native Mac mode on the hardware level, but the lack of QMK, VIA, or a web-based software solution means Mac and Linux users will struggle to remap secondary layers—a major feature needed on a 65% layout.

Internal Structure & Typing Experience

Under the hood, the AK650 uses a gasket mount design with silicon gasket jackets on a flex-cut polycarbonate plate. These jackets suspend the plate and PCB assembly to deliver an even, cushioned sound profile across the board. You get a 5-pin hot-swap PCB featuring south-facing RGB LEDs compatible with all standard MX-style switches. The 1.2mm flex-cut PCB uses high-quality flush sockets that greatly minimize the chance of shorting.

For switches, you have two linear options: Dreamweaving and Flying Fish (AJAZZ's own switches manufactured by Huano). Both are decently factory-lubed, smooth, and balanced nicely for gaming and typing. Combined with the board's internal foams and tuned stabilizers, it sounds remarkably "thocky" and deep right out of the box with zero modding required. If you are curious enough to open it up, you can easily pop open the top and bottom frames with a prying tool.

Connectivity & Battery Life

Powered by a massive 5000 mAh battery, the keyboard offers great endurance. You can expect around 150 hours of use on Bluetooth with RGB turned off, or roughly 25 hours with full RGB in 2.4GHz wireless mode. The polling rate reaches a responsive 1000Hz on Wired and 2.4GHz modes, dropping to 125Hz in Bluetooth mode.

Conclusion & Verdict

For $50, the AJAZZ AK650 is a feature-packed monster that punches way above its weight class. If you are a Windows user looking for a compact, wireless board featuring a display and a volume slider, it's a complete no-brainer. However, power users on Mac or Linux should keep the software limitations in mind until AJAZZ rolls out a promised web-based solution.

verdict: The Judicial Collab DK1 60% is an unusually distinctive custom keyboard that backs up its looks with excellent acoustics, flexible mounting options, and a genuinely enjoyable typing experience. description: A uniquely designed 60% custom keyboard with striking finishes and excellent sound.
metaDescription: A detailed review of the Judicial Collab DK1 60%, covering its unique marble-like design, mounting options, acoustics, PCB, build experience, and typing feel.
detailedDescription:
The Judicial Collab DK1 60% is one of the most distinctive 60% custom keyboards reviewed in its price range. Developed as a collaboration between Wu Studios and GD Lab, the DK1 60% combines a CNC-machined aluminum top case with multiple bottom-case, back-plate, layout, and mounting options, giving users considerable freedom to configure both its appearance and typing characteristics.

The standout feature is undoubtedly the case design. The anodized top case and aluminum weight use a marble-like “Marbalano” finish with shifting swirls and reflections that give the keyboard a different appearance from different angles. Slim bezels, an 8° typing angle, and a stainless-steel nameplate with dual PVD finishing further contribute to its distinctive look. Buyers can also choose between copper and brass bottom-case options, while the back plate is available in aluminum or copper with an engraved logo. These material choices also influence the keyboard's sound and resonance.

Inside, the DK1 60% uses a 1.6 mm non-flex-cut, 5-pin hot-swap PCB with south-facing switches and no RGB. It supports NKRO and a 1000 Hz polling rate in wired and 2.4 GHz modes, while the final wireless version is expected to use a 2400 mAh battery and tri-mode PCB. QMK support is also included for programming secondary layers and macros. The unified daughterboard connects to the PCB through a magnetic connector, making assembly more convenient.

The keyboard supports three layouts, including standard 60%, WKL, and HHKB configurations. Plate choices include polycarbonate, FR4, and aluminum, allowing users to tune the typing feel and acoustics. It also offers two primary mounting methods: plate-gasket mounting with silicone bolts for a softer and more flexible feel, and PCB-mounted gasket sleeves for a firmer typing experience. A hybrid configuration combining both mounting methods is also possible.

Acoustically, the DK1 60% is designed around a crisp, full, higher-pitched sound signature. Its bottom-case structure helps reduce unused cavity space and encourages resonance, resulting in a clean, high-pitched clack even without foam. Adding foam produces a deeper and more muted sound, giving users another way to tune the board. The final sound is heavily influenced by the selected switches, plate material, mounting configuration, and foam setup.

Despite the unusual choice of plate-mounted stabilizers for a $200 custom keyboard, the included stabilizers perform well according to the review. Users can also replace them with their preferred screw-in or clip-in stabilizers. The PCB's QMC hot-swap sockets were initially questionable at this price point, but their recessed contact design is intended to reduce the possibility of PCB shorting compared with sockets whose contacts extend outward.

Building the keyboard is described as straightforward and enjoyable, without unnecessary complexity. Daily use was equally positive, with the reviewer particularly impressed by both the appearance and typing experience. The main recommendation is to decide on the intended switches before ordering because certain switches may not pair particularly well with an aluminum plate.

The biggest drawback is availability. The DK1 60% is offered through a group buy rather than normal in-stock fulfillment, meaning missing the group-buy window could make obtaining the keyboard difficult until extras become available. The reviewer also did not have direct experience with several similarly priced competitors, so the review does not make a definitive head-to-head comparison.

Overall, the Judicial Collab DK1 60% stands out primarily through its design, customization options, and strong acoustic performance. Its unique finish makes it visually distinctive, while the different plates, mounting systems, materials, and foam configurations allow users to tailor the typing experience. For someone looking for an unusual 60% custom keyboard rather than a conventional in-stock option, the DK1 60% makes a compelling case.

name: Monka 3087 Pro V2
cons: Tape mod can make different switch configurations sound more similar
verdict: The Monka 3087 Pro V2 is a strong example of how well a good budget mechanical keyboard can age. At $40 / ৳4,000, it delivers a gasket mount, 1.6 mm PCB, solid stock switches, satisfying acoustics, tri-mode-style connectivity, and a large battery. The lack of QMK/VIA and north-facing LEDs are its main weaknesses, but neither is necessarily a dealbreaker at this price. For someone looking for an affordable TKL mechanical keyboard, particularly a first mechanical keyboard, the 3087 Pro V2 remains a very compelling option.
description: A feature-packed budget TKL with great switches, sound, and wireless connectivity.
metaDescription: The Monka 3087 Pro V2 remains a strong budget TKL mechanical keyboard thanks to its solid switches, gasket mount, full sound, and wireless connectivity.
detailedDescription:
The Monka 3087 Pro V2 is a budget TKL mechanical keyboard that originally launched around a year and a half before this review, yet continues to hold up surprisingly well at its $40 / ৳4,000 price point. While many newer keyboards have entered the budget market since its release, the 3087 Pro V2 still offers a combination of build features, stock switches, sound tuning, and wireless connectivity that makes it worth considering.

The keyboard uses a plastic case with Cherry-profile double-shot keycaps, a gasket-mounted construction, and a polycarbonate plate. Visually, it stands apart from many keyboards in the same price range with RGB side strips, an engraved Monka badge above the arrow keys, and an RGB diffuser. The thick keycaps also have distinctive fonts and give the board a more substantial appearance than its price might suggest.

One of its more interesting hardware choices is the 1.6 mm non-flex-cut hot-swap PCB. Unlike the increasingly common thin flex-cut PCBs, this design provides a firmer and more controlled typing experience when combined with the gasket mount. It also avoids excessive bounce and helps retain the keyboard's acoustic character. The PCB uses non-branded hot-swap sockets rather than Kailh or Gateron sockets, but the reviewer notes that similar sockets have performed reliably in other budget boards.

The stock switch selection is another major strength. Depending on the configuration, the 3087 Pro V2 can come with KD Wine Red, KD Higher Synth, or Monka Sea Salt Tactile switches. The KD linear switches are factory-lubed and provide a smooth, relatively balanced feel that works well for both everyday typing and gaming. The Sea Salt Tactile variant is particularly interesting because tactile switches are less common in pre-built keyboards at this price. Its moderate tactile bump and snappy return make it a versatile choice for users who prefer noticeable feedback.

Sound is another area where the 3087 Pro V2 performs particularly well. The keyboard uses a polycarbonate plate, tuned stabilizers, multiple layers of internal foam, and an unusual single-layer tape mod on the back of the PCB. The tape mod helps produce a fuller sound, although it can also make the different switch configurations sound somewhat more similar. Combined with the stock switches and acoustic tuning, the result is a fuller and more satisfying sound than would normally be expected from a plastic keyboard at this price.

There are, however, a couple of compromises. The north-facing RGB LEDs are somewhat unusual compared with the south-facing configuration that has become common on modern mechanical keyboards. This is not necessarily a problem, especially for users who prefer shine-through keycaps, but it can matter depending on the keycaps and switches being used.

The other major limitation is the lack of QMK/VIA support. The keyboard does have Windows software that allows users to remap keys, configure RGB lighting, and create macros, but it is not as convenient or platform-independent as VIA. The software is Windows-only, which limits functionality for native macOS and Linux users. On the positive side, the keyboard does include a dedicated Mac mode.

Connectivity is strong for the price, with wired, Bluetooth, and 2.4 GHz wireless modes, alongside a 4,000 mAh battery. This makes the board considerably more versatile as an everyday keyboard and gives it an advantage over many basic wired budget options.

Long-term reliability is also encouraging. The reviewer had used the keyboard for roughly a year and a half without encountering serious issues and had not heard widespread reports of major problems from other users. While that does not guarantee every unit will have the same experience, it is a positive sign for a budget board that has been on the market for some time.

Against similarly priced TKL keyboards such as the Lingo K87 and WKF WK87, the Monka 3087 Pro V2 remains competitive with its gasket mount, polycarbonate plate, good keycaps, wireless connectivity, and strong stock switches. The WKF WK87 has an advantage through its QMK/VIA support, but the 3087 Pro V2 still offers excellent value for users who prioritize sound, switch options, and overall usability.

At $40 / ৳4,000, the Monka 3087 Pro V2 is an easy recommendation for someone looking for an affordable first mechanical keyboard. The Sea Salt Tactile version is especially appealing to users coming from membrane keyboards who are accustomed to tactile feedback, while the linear options are also strong choices for general typing and gaming. Its combination of hardware, sound tuning, wireless connectivity, and proven reliability makes it a surprisingly capable budget TKL.
